audioscript.text: Part 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will hear a woman phoning a friend to get information about a job agency.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Hello, William.
audioscript.speaker: AMBER

audioscript.text: This is Amber.
audioscript.speaker: AMBER

audioscript.text: You said to phone if I wanted to get more information about the job agency you mentioned.
audioscript.speaker: AMBER

audioscript.text: Is now a good time?
audioscript.speaker: AMBER

audioscript.text: Uh. Hi, Amber.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: Yes, fine.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: So the agency I was talking about is called Bankside.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: They're based in Docklands.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: I can tell you the address now, 497 Eastside.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: OK, thanks.
audioscript.speaker: AMBER

audioscript.text: So is there anyone in particular I should speak to there?
audioscript.speaker: AMBER

audioscript.text: The agent I always deal with is called Becky Jamieson.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: Let me write that down.
audioscript.speaker: AMBER

audioscript.text: Becky...
audioscript.speaker: AMBER

audioscript.text: Jamieson.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM
audioscript.explain: Q1: The passage says the agent's name is *'Jamieson'* and spells it *'JAMIESON'*. So the answer is **Jamieson**.

audioscript.text: JAMIESON.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM
audioscript.explain: Q1: The passage says the agent's name is *'Jamieson'* and spells it *'JAMIESON'*. So the answer is **Jamieson**.

audioscript.text: Do you have her direct line?
audioscript.speaker: AMBER

audioscript.text: Yes, it's in my contacts somewhere.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: Right, here we are.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: I wouldn't call her until the afternoon, if I were you.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM
audioscript.explain: Q2: The passage says *'I wouldn't call her until the afternoon'* — **'until the afternoon'** means the best time is the afternoon. So the answer is **afternoon**.

audioscript.text: She's always really busy in the morning, trying to fill last-minute vacancies.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: She's really helpful and friendly, so I'm sure it would be worth getting in touch with her for an informal chat.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: It's mainly clerical and admin jobs they deal with, isn't it?
audioscript.speaker: AMBER

audioscript.text: That's right.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: I know you're hoping to find a full-time job in the media eventually, but Becky mostly recruits temporary staff for the finance sector.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: Which will look good on your Cv, and generally pays better too.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: Yeah, I'm just a bit worried because I don't have much office experience.
audioscript.speaker: AMBER

audioscript.text: I wouldn't worry.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: They'll probably start you as a receptionist or something like that.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: So what's important for that kind of job isn't so much having business skills or knowing lots of different computer systems.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: It's communication that really matters, so you'd be fine there.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM
audioscript.explain: Q3: The passage says *'It's communication that really matters'* — **'really matters'** means it is the most important skill. So the answer is **communication**.

audioscript.text: And you'll pick up office skills really quickly on the job.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: It's not that complicated.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: OK, good.
audioscript.speaker: AMBER

audioscript.text: So, how long do people generally need temporary staff for?
audioscript.speaker: AMBER

audioscript.text: It would be great if I could get something lasting at least a month.
audioscript.speaker: AMBER

audioscript.text: That shouldn't be too difficult.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: But you're more likely to be offered something for a week at first, which might get extended.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM
audioscript.explain: Q4: The passage says you are *'more likely to be offered something for a week at first'* — **'at first'** means the starting length. So the answer is **week**.

audioscript.text: It's unusual to be sent somewhere for just a day or two.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: Right.
audioscript.speaker: AMBER

audioscript.text: I've heard the pay isn't too bad.
audioscript.speaker: AMBER

audioscript.text: Better than working in a shop or a restaurant.
audioscript.speaker: AMBER

audioscript.text: Oh, yes, definitely.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: The hourly rate is about 10 pounds, 11 if you're lucky.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM
audioscript.explain: Q5: The passage says *'The hourly rate is about 10 pounds'* — **'hourly rate'** means pay per hour. So the answer is **10**.

audioscript.text: That's pretty good.
audioscript.speaker: AMBER

audioscript.text: I was only expecting to get 8 or 9 pounds an hour.
audioscript.speaker: AMBER

audioscript.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Listen and answer questions 6 to 10.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Do you want me to tell you anything about the registration process?
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: Yes, please.
audioscript.speaker: AMBER

audioscript.text: I know you have to have an interview.
audioscript.speaker: AMBER

audioscript.text: The interview usually takes about an hour, and you should arrange that about a week in advance.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: I suppose I should dress smartly, if it's for office work.
audioscript.speaker: AMBER

audioscript.text: I can probably borrow a suit from Mum.
audioscript.speaker: AMBER
audioscript.explain: Q6: The passage says *'I can probably borrow a suit from Mum'* — **'suit'** is the smart clothing for the interview. So the answer is **suit**.

audioscript.text: Good idea, it's better to look too smart than too casual.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: Will I need to bring copies of my exam certificates or anything like that?
audioscript.speaker: AMBER

audioscript.text: No, they don't need to see those, I don't think.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: What about my passport?
audioscript.speaker: AMBER

audioscript.text: Oh, yes, they will ask to see that.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM
audioscript.explain: Q7: The passage says they *'will ask to see'* your passport — **'ask to see'** means you must bring it. So the answer is **passport**.

audioscript.text: OK.
audioscript.speaker: AMBER

audioscript.text: I wouldn't get stressed about the interview though.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: It's just a chance for them to build relationship with you, so they can try and match you to a job which you'll like.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: So there are questions about personality that they always ask candidates.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM
audioscript.explain: Q8: The passage says *'there are questions about personality that they always ask'* — **'always ask'** means it is a regular topic. So the answer is **personality**.

audioscript.text: Fairly basic ones, and they probably won't ask anything too difficult, like what your plans are for the future.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: Hope not.
audioscript.speaker: AMBER

audioscript.text: Anyway, there are lots of benefits to using an agency.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: For example, the interview will be useful because they'll give you feedback on your performance, so you can improve next time.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM
audioscript.explain: Q9: The passage says *'they'll give you feedback on your performance'* — **'give you feedback'** means you receive it. So the answer is **feedback**.

audioscript.text: And they'll have access to jobs which aren't advertised.
audioscript.speaker: AMBER

audioscript.text: Exactly, most temporary jobs aren't advertised.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: And I expect finding a temporary job this way takes a lot less time, it's much easier than ringing up individual companies.
audioscript.speaker: AMBER
audioscript.explain: Q10: The passage says finding a job this way *'takes a lot less time'* — **'less time'** means it is faster and easier. So the answer is **time**.

audioscript.text: Yes, indeed.
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: Well, I think I've covered...
audioscript.speaker: WILLIAM

audioscript.text: That is the end of part 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Part 2.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will hear a woman giving a presentation about a holiday on an island in Britain that her company organizes.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Good morning.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

audioscript.text: My name's Erica Matthews, and I'm the owner of Matthews Island Holidays, a company set up by my parents.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

audioscript.text: Thank you for coming to this presentation, in which I hope to interest you in what we have to offer.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

audioscript.text: We're a small family-run company, and we believe in the importance of the personal touch.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

audioscript.text: So we don't aim to compete with other companies on the number of customers.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

audioscript.text: What we do is build on our many years' experience, more than almost any other rail holiday company,
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS
audioscript.explain: Q11: The passage says the company has *'many years' experience, more than almost any other rail holiday company'* — **'more than almost any other'** means they have been in business **longer** than most competitors. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: to ensure we provide perfect holidays in a small number of destinations, which we've got to know extremely well.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

audioscript.text: I'll start with our six-day Isle of Man holiday.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

audioscript.text: This is a fascinating island in the Irish Sea, with Wales to the south, England to the east, Scotland to the north, and Northern Ireland to the west.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

audioscript.text: Our holiday starts in Heysham, where your tour manager will meet you.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS
audioscript.explain: Q12: The passage says *'Our holiday starts in Heysham, where your tour manager will meet you'* — this directly tells you the meeting place is **Heysham**. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: Then you'll travel by ferry to the Isle of Man.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

audioscript.text: Some people prefer to fly from Luton instead.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

audioscript.text: And another popular option is to go by train to Liverpool and take a ferry from there.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

audioscript.text: You have five nights in the hotel, and the price covers five breakfasts and dinners.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

audioscript.text: And lunch on the three days when there are organized trips.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS
audioscript.explain: Q13: The passage says *'lunch on the three days when there are organized trips'* — this means exactly **three** lunches are included. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: Day 4 is free, and most people have lunch in a cafe or restaurant in Douglas.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

audioscript.text: The price of the holiday includes the ferry to the Isle of Man, all travel on the island, the hotel, and the meals I've mentioned.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

audioscript.text: Incidentally, we try to make booking our holidays as simple and fair as possible.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

audioscript.text: So unlike with many companies, the price is the same, whether you book 6 months in advance or at the last minute, and there's no supplement for single rooms in hotels.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

audioscript.text: If you make a booking, then need to change the start date, for example because of illness, you're welcome to change to an alternative date or a different tour for a small administrative fee.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS
audioscript.explain: Q14: The passage says if you change the start date, you pay *'a small administrative fee'* — this means you pay **extra** for **transferring to another date**. ***Option A is a trap*** — the passage says there is *'no supplement for single rooms'*, so larger rooms are not mentioned. So the answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: OK, so what does the holiday consist of?
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

audioscript.text: Well, on day one, you'll arrive in time for a short introduction by your tour manager, followed by dinner in the hotel.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

audioscript.text: The dining room looks out at the river, close to where it flows into the harbor, and there's usually plenty of activity going on.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS
audioscript.explain: Q15: The passage says *'The dining room looks out at the river'* — the view from the hotel dining room is of the **river**. So the answer is **river**.

audioscript.text: On day two, you'll take the coach to the small town of Peel,
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

audioscript.text: on the way calling in at the Tynwald Exhibition.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

audioscript.text: The Isle of Man isn't part of the United Kingdom, and it has its own parliament called Tynwald.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

audioscript.text: It's claimed that this is the world's oldest parliament that's still functioning, and that it dates back to 979.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

audioscript.text: However, the earliest surviving reference to it is from 1422, so, perhaps it isn't quite as old as it claims.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS
audioscript.explain: Q16: The passage says *'the earliest surviving reference to it is from 1422'* — this means Tynwald may have been founded in **1422**, not 979. So the answer is **1422**.

audioscript.text: Day three, we have a trip to the mountain Snaefell.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

audioscript.text: This begins with a leisurely ride along the promenade in Douglas in a horse-drawn tram.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

audioscript.text: Then you board an electric train, which takes you to the fishing village of Laxey.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

audioscript.text: From there, it's an eight-kilometer ride in the Snaefell Mountain Railway to the top.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS
audioscript.explain: Q17: The passage says you take the Snaefell Mountain Railway *'to the top'* — the train goes to the **top** of Snaefell. So the answer is **top**.

audioscript.text: Lunch will be in the cafe, giving you spectacular views of the island.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS

audioscript.text: Day 4 is free for you to explore, using the pass which we'll give you.
audioscript.speaker: ERICA MATTHEWS
audioscript.explain: Q18: The passage says on Day 4 you explore *'using the pass which we'll give you'* — the company provides a **pass** for local transport and heritage sites. So the answer is **pass**.

audioscript.text: So you won't have to pay for travel on local transport, or for entrance to the island's heritage sites.

audioscript.text: You will hear a student giving a presentation about a type of tree known as the eucalyptus, which is common in Australia.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Today, I'm going to talk about the eucalyptus tree.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This is a very common tree here in Australia, where it's also sometimes called the gum tree.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: First, I'm going to talk about why it's important.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Then I'm going to describe some problems it faces at present.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Right, well, the eucalyptus tree is an important tree for lots of reasons.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: For example, it gives shelter to creatures like birds and bats.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The passage says the eucalyptus *'gives shelter to creatures like birds and bats'* — **'gives'** here means it provides something. So the answer is **shelter**.

audioscript.text: And these and other species also depend on it for food, particularly the nectar from its flowers.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So it supports biodiversity.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It's useful to us humans too, because we can kill germs with a disinfectant made from oil extracted from eucalyptus leaves.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The passage says a disinfectant is *'made from oil extracted from eucalyptus leaves'* — the leaves give us this **oil**. So the answer is **oil**.

audioscript.text: The eucalyptus grows all over Australia, and the trees can live for up to 400 years.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So it's alarming that all across the country, numbers of eucalyptus are falling.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Because the trees are dying off prematurely.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So what are the reasons for this?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: One possible reason is disease.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As far back as the 1970s the trees started getting a disease called Mundulla Yellows.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The trees' leaves would gradually turn yellow then the tree would die.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It wasn't until 2004 that they found the cause of the problem was lime, or calcium hydroxide to give it its proper chemical name.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Which was being used in the construction of roads.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage says lime *'was being used in the construction of roads'* — **'construction'** means making something. So the answer is **roads**.

audioscript.text: The lime was being washed away into the ground and affecting the roots of the eucalyptus trees nearby.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: What it was doing was preventing the trees from sucking up the iron they needed for healthy growth.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: When this was injected back into the affected trees, they immediately recovered.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But this problem only affected a relatively small number of trees.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: By 2000, huge numbers of eucalyptus were dying along Australia's East Coast.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Of a disease known as Bell-miner Associated Die-back.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The bell-miner is a bird, and the disease seems to be common where there are high populations of bell-miners.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Again, it's the leaves of the trees that are affected.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: What happens is that insects settle on the leaves and eat their way round them.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage says *'insects settle on the leaves and eat their way round them'* — **'settle on'** and **'eat'** together mean they **feed** on the leaves. So the answer is **insects**.

audioscript.text: Destroying them as they go, and at the same time, they secrete a solution which has sugar in it.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The bell-miner birds really like this solution, and in order to get as much as possible, they keep away other creatures that might try to get it.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So these birds and insects flourish at the expense of other species, and eventually so much damage is done to the leaves that the tree dies.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But experts say that trees can start looking sick before any sign of bell-miner associated dieback.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So, it looks as if the problem might have another explanation.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: One possibility is that it's to do with the huge bushfires that we have in Australia.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: A theory proposed over 40 years ago by ecologist William Jackson is that the frequency of bushfires in a particular region affects the type of vegetation that grows there.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: If there are very frequent bushfires in a region, this encourages grass to grow afterwards, while if the bushfires are rather less frequent, this results in the growth of eucalyptus forests.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The passage says high-frequency fires *'encourages grass to grow'* — **'encourages'** means it causes this result. So the answer is **grass**.

audioscript.text: So why is this?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Why do fairly frequent bushfires actually support the growth of eucalyptus?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Well, one reason is that the fire stops the growth of other species which would consume water needed by eucalyptus trees.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q36: The passage says fire stops other species that *'would consume water needed by eucalyptus trees'* — **'consume'** means use up, so fire makes more **water** available. So the answer is **water**.

audioscript.text: And there's another reason.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: If these other quick-growing species of bushes and plants are allowed to proliferate, they harm the eucalyptus in another way.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: By affecting the composition of the soil and removing nutrients from it.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q37: The passage says other plants harm eucalyptus by *'affecting the composition of the soil'* — **'composition'** means the quality or makeup of something. So the answer is **soil**.

audioscript.text: So some bushfires are actually essential for the eucalyptus to survive, as long as they are not too frequent.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In fact, there's evidence that Australia's indigenous people practiced regular burning of bushland for thousands of years.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Before the arrival of the Europeans.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But since Europeans arrived on the continent, the number of bushfires has been strictly controlled.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Now scientists believe that this reduced frequency of bushfires to low levels has led to what's known as dry rainforest, which seems an odd name, as usually we associate tropical rainforest with wet conditions.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q38: The passage says low-frequency fires led to *'dry rainforest'* — the question asks for the type of rainforest, and the passage directly names it. So the answer is **dry**.

audioscript.text: And what's special about this type of rainforest?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Well, unlike tropical rainforest, which is a rich ecosystem, this type of ecosystem is usually a simple one.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q39: The passage says this type of ecosystem *'is usually a simple one'* — **'simple'** directly describes the ecosystem. So the answer is **simple**.

audioscript.text: It has very thick dense vegetation, but not much variety of species.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The vegetation provides lots of shade, so one species that does find it ideal is the bell-miner bird.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Which builds its nests in the undergrowth there, but again, that's not helpful for the eucalyptus tree.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q40: The passage says the bell-miner *'builds its nests in the undergrowth there'* — the question asks for an ideal environment for the bell-miner's **nests**. So the answer is **nests**.

audioscript.text: That is the end of part 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.

audioscript.text: I'm very pleased to welcome this evening's guest speaker, Mark Logan, who's going to tell us about the recent transformation of Minster Park.

audioscript.text: I'm sure you're all familiar with Minster Park.
audioscript.speaker: MARK

audioscript.text: It's been a feature of the city for well over a century, and has been the responsibility of the city council for most of that time.
audioscript.speaker: MARK

audioscript.text: What perhaps isn't so well known is the origin of the park.
audioscript.speaker: MARK

audioscript.text: Unlike many public parks that started in private ownership, as the garden of a large house for instance, Minster was some waste land, which people living nearby started planting with flowers in 1892.
audioscript.speaker: MARK
audioscript.explain: Q11: The passage says Minster Park started when *'people living nearby started planting with flowers in 1892'* on *'waste land'*. This means local people created it together — **'people living nearby'** matches **'local community'**, and **'started planting'** matches **'set up'**. So the answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: It was unclear who actually owned the land.
audioscript.speaker: MARK

audioscript.text: And this wasn't settled until 20 years later, when the council took possession of it.
audioscript.speaker: MARK

audioscript.text: You may have noticed the statue near one of the entrances.
audioscript.speaker: MARK

audioscript.text: It's of Diane Gosforth, who played a key role in the history of the park.
audioscript.speaker: MARK

audioscript.text: Once the council had become the legal owner, it planned to sell the land for housing.
audioscript.speaker: MARK

audioscript.text: Many local people wanted it to remain a place that everyone could go to, to enjoy the fresh air and natural environment.
audioscript.speaker: MARK

audioscript.text: Remember, the park is in a densely populated residential area.
audioscript.speaker: MARK

audioscript.text: Diane Gosforth was one of those people, and she organized petitions and demonstrations, which eventually made the council change its mind about the future of the land.
audioscript.speaker: MARK
audioscript.explain: Q12: The passage says Diane Gosforth *'organized petitions and demonstrations'* to stop the council from selling the land. **'Organized petitions and demonstrations'** means she **'helped to lead a campaign'**. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: You will hear part of a presentation about an agricultural program in the country of Mozambique.

audioscript.text: I'm going to report on a case study of a program which has been set up to help rural populations in Mozambique, a largely agricultural country in Southeast Africa.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The program worked with three communities in Chicualacuala district near the Limpopo River.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This is a dry and arid region with unpredictable rainfall.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Because of this, people in the area were unable to support themselves through agriculture, and instead they used the forest,
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: as a means of providing themselves with an income, mainly by selling charcoal.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: However, this was not a sustainable way of living in the long term, as they were rapidly using up this resource.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: To support agriculture in this dry region, the program focused primarily on making use of existing water resources from the Limpopo River,
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The passage says the program *'focused primarily on making use of existing water resources'* by *'setting up systems of irrigation'*. The question asks for the main priority to ensure water supply — **'irrigation'** is the system that provides water. So the answer is **irrigation**.

audioscript.text: by setting up systems of irrigation, which would provide a dependable water supply for crops and animals.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The program worked closely with the district government in order to find the best way of implementing this.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The region already had one farmers' association, and it was decided to set up two more of these.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: These associations planned and carried out activities, including water management, livestock breeding and agriculture.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And it was notable that in general, women formed the majority of the workforce.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The passage states *'women formed the majority of the workforce'* — **'majority'** means most of the workers. The question asks who did most of the work, so the answer is **women**.

audioscript.text: It was decided that in order to keep the crops safe from animals, both wild and domestic, special areas should be fenced off.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Where the crops could be grown.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The community was responsible for creating these fences, but the program provided the necessary wire for making them.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage says the program *'provided the necessary wire for making them'* — **'them'** refers to the fences. So the program provided **wire** for the fences.

audioscript.text: Once the area had been fenced off, it could be cultivated.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The land was dug, so that vegetables and cereals appropriate to the climate could be grown, and the program provided the necessary seeds for this.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage says the program *'provided the necessary seeds for this'* — **'this'** means growing vegetables and cereals. So the program provided **seeds** for suitable crops.

audioscript.text: The program also provided pumps, so that water could be brought from the river in pipes to the fields.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: However, the labor was all provided by local people, and they also provided and put up the posts that supported the fences around the fields.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The passage says local people *'provided and put up the posts that supported the fences'*. The question asks what farmers provided for the fences — the answer is **posts**.

audioscript.text: Once the program had been set up, its development was monitored carefully.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The farmers were able to grow enough produce, not just for their own needs,
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: but also to sell.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: However, getting the produce to places where it could be marketed was sometimes a problem, as the farmers did not have access to transport.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q36: The passage says *'the farmers did not have access to transport'*, which made marketing produce difficult. The question asks for the reason marketing was hard — the lack of **transport**.

audioscript.text: And this resulted in large amounts of produce, especially vegetables, being spoiled.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This problem was discussed with the farmers' associations, and it was decided that in order to prevent food from being spoiled.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The farmers needed to learn techniques for its preservation.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q37: The passage says farmers needed to *'learn techniques for its preservation'* to stop food from spoiling. The question asks about training in methods of food **preservation**.

audioscript.text: There was also an additional initiative that had not been originally planned, but which became a central feature of the program.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This was when farmers started to dig holes for tanks in the fenced-off areas, and to fill these with water, and use them for breeding fish, an important source of protein.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q38: The passage says farmers dug holes, filled them with water, and used them *'for breeding fish'*. The question asks what was kept in these special places — the answer is **fish**.

audioscript.text: After a time, another suggestion was made by local people, which hadn't been part of the program's original proposal.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But which was also adopted later on.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: They decided to try setting up colonies of bees, which would provide honey, both for their own consumption and to sell.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q39: The passage says local people suggested *'setting up colonies of bees'* for honey. The question asks what they later suggested keeping — the answer is **bees**.

audioscript.text: So what lessons can be learned from this program?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: First of all, it tells us that in dry, arid regions, if there is access to a reliable source of water,
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: there is great potential for the development of agriculture.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In Chicualacuala, there was a marked improvement in agricultural production,
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: which improved food security and benefited local people by providing them with both food and income.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: However, it's important to set realistic timelines for each phase of the program, especially for its design.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q40: The passage says it's important to set realistic timelines *'especially for its design'* phase. The question asks which phase needs enough time — the answer is **design**.

audioscript.text: As mistakes made at this stage may be hard to correct later on.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The program demonstrates that sustainable development is possible in areas where there is...

audioscript.text: My guest on the show today is Alice Riches, who started the street play scheme where she lives in Beechwood Road.
audioscript.speaker: PRESENTER

audioscript.text: For those of you that don't already know, street play involves local residents closing off their street for a few hours so that children have a chance to play in the street safely.
audioscript.speaker: PRESENTER

audioscript.text: She started it in her own street, Beechwood Road, and the idea caught on, and there are now street play schemes all over the city.
audioscript.speaker: PRESENTER

audioscript.text: So when did you actually start the scheme, Alice?
audioscript.speaker: PRESENTER

audioscript.text: Well, I first had the idea when my oldest child was still a toddler.
audioscript.speaker: ALICE

audioscript.text: So that's about oh, 6 years ago now, but it took at least 2 years of campaigning before we were actually able to make it happen.
audioscript.speaker: ALICE

audioscript.text: So the scheme's been up and running for 3 years now.
audioscript.speaker: ALICE
audioscript.explain: Q11: The passage says the scheme *'has been up and running for 3 years now'* — **'up and running'** means it has been happening. So the first time was **three years ago**.

audioscript.text: We'd love to be able to close our road for longer, for the whole weekend from Saturday morning until Sunday evening for example.
audioscript.speaker: ALICE

audioscript.text: At the moment, it's just once a week, but when we started, it was only once a month, but we're working on it.
audioscript.speaker: ALICE
audioscript.explain: Q12: Alice says *'At the moment, it's just once a week'* — **'at the moment'** means **now**. So the road is closed **once a week**.

audioscript.text: So what actually happens when Beechwood Road is closed?
audioscript.speaker: PRESENTER

audioscript.text: We have volunteer wardens.
audioscript.speaker: ALICE

audioscript.text: Mostly parents, but some elderly residents too, who block off our road at either end.
audioscript.speaker: ALICE
audioscript.explain: Q13: The passage says *'We have volunteer wardens'* who *'block off our road'* — **'block off'** means **close**. So **local wardens** are responsible.

audioscript.text: The council have provided special signs, but there's always a volunteer there to explain what's happening to any motorists.
audioscript.speaker: ALICE

audioscript.text: Generally they're fine about it.
audioscript.speaker: ALICE

audioscript.text: We've only had to get the police involved once or twice.
audioscript.speaker: ALICE

audioscript.text: Now, I should explain that the road isn't completely closed to cars.
audioscript.speaker: ALICE

audioscript.text: But only residents' cars are allowed.
audioscript.speaker: ALICE

audioscript.text: If people really need to get in or out of Beechwood Road, it's not a problem, as long as they drive at under 20 km per hour.

audioscript.text: So, can anyone apply to get involved in street play?

audioscript.text: Absolutely.
audioscript.speaker: ALICE

audioscript.text: We want to include all kids in the city, especially those who live on busy roads.

audioscript.text: Part 3.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will hear two students called Hazel and Tom talking about Hazel's media studies assignment.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Tom, could I ask you for some advice, please?
audioscript.speaker: HAZEL

audioscript.text: Yes, of course.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: If you think I can help.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: What's it about?
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: It's my first media studies assignment, and I'm not sure how to go about it.
audioscript.speaker: HAZEL

audioscript.text: You must have done it last year.
audioscript.speaker: HAZEL

audioscript.text: Is that the one comparing the coverage of a particular story in a range of newspapers?
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: That's right.
audioscript.speaker: HAZEL

audioscript.text: Oh yes, I really enjoyed writing it.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: So, what sort of things do I need to compare?
audioscript.speaker: HAZEL

audioscript.text: Well, there are several things.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: For example, there's the question of which page of the newspaper the item appears on.
audioscript.speaker: TOM
audioscript.explain: Q21: The passage asks *'which page of the newspaper the item appears on'* — this directly tells you what to check. So the answer is **page**.

audioscript.text: You mean because there's a big difference between having it on the front page and the bottom of page 10 for instance?
audioscript.speaker: HAZEL

audioscript.text: Exactly.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: And that shows how important the editor thinks the story is.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: Then there's the size, how many column inches the story is given, how many columns it spreads over.
audioscript.speaker: TOM
audioscript.explain: Q22: The passage says *'Then there's the size, how many column inches the story is given'* — **'size'** is the exact word used. So the answer is **size**.

audioscript.text: And I suppose that includes the headline.
audioscript.speaker: HAZEL

audioscript.text: It certainly does.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: It's all part of attracting the reader's attention.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: What about graphics?
audioscript.speaker: HAZEL

audioscript.text: Whether there's anything visual in addition to the text?
audioscript.speaker: HAZEL
audioscript.explain: Q23: The passage asks *'Whether there's anything visual in addition to the text?'* — **'visual'** things like pictures are called **graphics**. So the answer is **graphics**.

audioscript.text: Yes, you need to consider those too.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: Because they can have a big effect on the reader's understanding of the story, sometimes a bigger effect than the text itself.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: Then you'll need to look at how the item is put together.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: What structure is it given?
audioscript.speaker: TOM
audioscript.explain: Q24: The passage asks *'What structure is it given?'* — **'structure'** means how the item is organized. So the answer is **structure**.

audioscript.text: Bear in mind that not many people read beyond the first paragraph, so what has the journalist put at the beginning?
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: And if say there are conflicting opinions about something, does one appear near the end, where people probably won't read it?
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: And newspapers sometimes give wrong or misleading information, don't they?
audioscript.speaker: HAZEL

audioscript.text: Either deliberately or by accident, should I be looking at that too?
audioscript.speaker: HAZEL

audioscript.text: Yes, if you can, compare what's in different versions, and as far as possible.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: Try and work out what's true and what isn't, and that relates to a very important point.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: What's the writer's purpose?
audioscript.speaker: TOM
audioscript.explain: Q25: The passage asks *'What's the writer's purpose?'* — **'purpose'** is the writer's main goal or reason. So the answer is **purpose**.

audioscript.text: Or at least the most important one, if they have several.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: It may seem to be to inform the public, but often it's that they want to create fear.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: Or controversy, or to make somebody look ridiculous.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: Gosh, I see what you mean.
audioscript.speaker: HAZEL

audioscript.text: And I suppose the writer may make assumptions about the reader.
audioscript.speaker: HAZEL
audioscript.explain: Q26: The passage says *'the writer may make assumptions about the reader'* — **'assumptions'** are things the writer believes without proof. So the answer is **assumptions**.

audioscript.text: That's right, about their knowledge of the subject, their attitudes, and their level of education, which means writing so that the readers understand without feeling patronized.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: All of that will make a difference to how the story is presented.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Does it matter what type of story I write about?
audioscript.speaker: HAZEL

audioscript.text: No, national or international politics, the arts, anything.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: As long as it's covered in two or three newspapers, though of course it'll be easier and more fun if it's something you're interested in, and know something about.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: And on that basis, a national news item would be worth analyzing.
audioscript.speaker: HAZEL
audioscript.explain: Q27: Hazel says *'a national news item would be worth analyzing'* — **'worth analyzing'** means she will definitely look for one. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: I'm quite keen on politics, so I'll try and find a suitable topic.
audioscript.speaker: HAZEL

audioscript.text: What did you choose for your analysis, Tom?
audioscript.speaker: HAZEL

audioscript.text: I was interested in how newspapers express their opinions explicitly.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: So, I wanted to compare editorials in different papers, but when I started looking, I couldn't find two on the same topic that I felt like analyzing.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: In that case, I wouldn't even bother to look.
audioscript.speaker: HAZEL
audioscript.explain: Q28: Tom says about editorials: *'I wouldn't even bother to look'* — **'wouldn't bother'** means he definitely won't search. So the answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: So in the end, I chose a human interest story, a terribly emotional story about a young girl who was very ill.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: And lots of other people, mostly strangers, raised money so she could go abroad for treatment.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: Actually, I was surprised.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: Some papers just wrote about how wonderful everyone was.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: But others considered the broader picture, like why treatment wasn't available here.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: Hmm, I usually find stories like that raise quite strong feelings in me.
audioscript.speaker: HAZEL

audioscript.text: I'll avoid that.
audioscript.speaker: HAZEL
audioscript.explain: Q29: Hazel says about human interest stories: *'I'll avoid that'* — **'avoid'** means she definitely won't look for one. So the answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: Perhaps I'll choose an arts topic, like different reviews of a film or something about funding for the arts.
audioscript.speaker: HAZEL
audioscript.explain: Q30: Hazel says *'Perhaps I'll choose an arts topic'* — **'Perhaps'** means she may look for one, but she's not sure. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: I'll think about that.
audioscript.speaker: HAZEL

audioscript.text: Yes, that might be interesting.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: OK, well, thanks a lot for your help, Tom.
audioscript.speaker: HAZEL

audioscript.text: It's been really useful.
audioscript.speaker: HAZEL

audioscript.text: You're welcome.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: Good luck with the assignment, Hazel.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: That is the end of part 3.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have 30 seconds to check your answers to part 3.

audioscript.text: Part 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will hear part of a lecture on the early history of keeping clean.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Nowadays, we use different products for personal cleanliness, laundry, dishwashing, and household cleaning.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But this is very much a 20th-century development.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The origins of cleanliness date back to prehistoric times.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Since water is essential for life, the earliest people lived near water and knew something about its cleansing properties.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: At least that it rinsed MUD off their hands.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The passage says early people knew water *'rinsed MUD off their hands'* — **'rinsed off'** means **'washed off'**. So the answer is **mud**.

audioscript.text: During the excavation of ancient Babylon, evidence was found that soap making was known.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As early as 2800 BC, archaeologists discovered cylinders made of clay with inscriptions on them saying that fats were boiled with ashes.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The passage says archaeologists found *'cylinders made of clay'* with soap-making inscriptions — **'made of clay'** means the cylinders were **clay** cylinders. So the answer is **clay**.

audioscript.text: This is a method of making soap, though there's no reference to the purpose of this material.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The early Greeks bathed for aesthetic reasons, and apparently didn't use soap.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Instead, they cleaned their bodies with blocks of sand, pumice, and ashes.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Then anointed themselves with oil, and scraped off the oil and dirt with a metal instrument known as a strigil.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage describes a *'metal instrument known as a strigil'* — **'instrument'** means **'scraper'** here. So the strigil was made of **metal**.

audioscript.text: They also used oil mixed with ashes.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Clothes were washed without soap in streams.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The ancient Germans and Gauls are also credited with discovering how to make a substance called soap, made of melted animal fat and ashes. They used this mixture to tint their hair red.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage says ancient Germans and Gauls used soap *'to tint their hair red'* — **'tint'** means **'colour'**. So they coloured their **hair**.

audioscript.text: Soap got its name according to an ancient Roman legend from Mount Sapo, where animals were sacrificed, leaving deposits of animal fat.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Rain washed these deposits along with wood ashes down into the clay soil along the river Tiber.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Women found that this mixture greatly reduced the effort required to wash their clothes.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As Roman civilization advanced, so did bathing.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The first of the famous Roman baths, supplied with water from their aqueducts, was built around 312 BC.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The passage says *'the first of the famous Roman baths'* was built around 312 BC, supplied by aqueducts — **'baths'** are the place the water was carried to. So the answer is **baths**.

audioscript.text: The baths were luxurious, and bathing became very popular.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And by the second century AD,
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: the Greek physician Galen recommended soap for both medicinal and cleansing purposes.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: After the fall of Rome in 467 AD, and the resulting decline in bathing habits, much of Europe felt the impact of filth on public health.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This lack of personal cleanliness and related unsanitary living conditions were major factors in the outbreaks of disease in the Middle Ages.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q36: The passage says lack of cleanliness was a major factor in *'outbreaks of disease'* — **'outbreaks'** means **'occurrence'**. So the decline in bathing contributed to **diseases**.

audioscript.text: And especially the Black Death of the 14th century.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Nevertheless, soap making became an established craft in Europe, and associations of soap makers guarded their trade secrets closely.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Vegetable and animal oils were used with ashes of plants, along with perfume, apparently for the first time.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q37: The passage says soap makers used oils and ashes *'along with perfume, apparently for the first time'* — this means **perfume** was a new addition. So the answer is **perfume**.

audioscript.text: Gradually, more varieties of soap became available for shaving and shampooing.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As well as bathing and laundering.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: A major step toward large scale commercial soap making occurred in 1791 when a French chemist Nicholas LeBlanc patented a process for turning salt into soda ash, or sodium carbonate.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q38: The passage says LeBlanc patented a process for *'turning salt into soda ash'* — **'turning... into'** means **'making... from'**. So he made soda ash from **salt**.

audioscript.text: Soda ash is the alkali obtained from ashes that combines with fat to form soap.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The LeBlanc process yielded quantities of good quality inexpensive soda ash.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Modern soap making was born some 20 years later, in the early 19th century, with the discovery by Michel Eugène Chevreul, another French chemist, of the chemical nature and relationship of fats, glycerin, and fatty acids.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: His studies established the basis for both fat and soap chemistry.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And soap making became a science.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q39: The passage says after Chevreul's studies, *'soap making became a science'* — **'became'** means **'turned into'**. So he turned soapmaking into a **science**.

audioscript.text: Further developments during the 19th century made it easier and cheaper to manufacture soap.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Until the 19th century, soap was regarded as a luxury item, and was heavily taxed in several countries.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As it became more readily available, it became an everyday necessity.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: A development that was reinforced when the high tax was removed.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q40: The passage says soap became an everyday necessity when *'the high tax was removed'* — **'removed'** means there was no longer a **tax**. So the answer is **tax**.

audioscript.text: Soap was then something ordinary people could afford, and cleanliness standards improved.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: With this widespread use came the development of milder soaps for bathing, and soaps for use in the washing machines that were available to consumers by the turn of the 20th century.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That is the end of part 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: We're doing a customer satisfaction survey.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Yes, OK.

audioscript.text: I've got about 10 minutes before my train home leaves.
audioscript.speaker: SOPHIE

audioscript.text: I'm on a day trip.
audioscript.speaker: SOPHIE

audioscript.text: Great, thank you.

audioscript.text: So first of all, could you tell me your name?

audioscript.text: It's Sophie Bird.

audioscript.text: Thank you.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: And would you mind telling me what you do?
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: I'm a journalist.
audioscript.speaker: SOPHIE

audioscript.text: Oh, really?
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: That must be interesting.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Yes, it is.
audioscript.speaker: SOPHIE

audioscript.text: So, what's the reason for your visit here today?
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Work?
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Actually, it's my day off.
audioscript.speaker: SOPHIE

audioscript.text: I came here to do some shopping.
audioscript.speaker: SOPHIE
audioscript.explain: Q2: The man asks if her visit is for *'Work?'* but Sophie says *'Actually, it's my day off'* and *'I came here to do some shopping'*. So the reason is **shopping**.

audioscript.text: But I do sometimes come here for work.
audioscript.speaker: SOPHIE

audioscript.text: OK.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Yes, no problem.
audioscript.speaker: SOPHIE

audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Staunfirth, where I live.
audioscript.speaker: SOPHIE

audioscript.text: Uh. Can I just check the spelling?
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: STAUNFIRTH?
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: That's right.
audioscript.speaker: SOPHIE

audioscript.text: Hmm. And you traveled from there this morning?
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Yes.
audioscript.speaker: SOPHIE

audioscript.text: OK, good.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Next, can I ask what kind of ticket you bought?
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: I assume it wasn't a season ticket, as you don't travel every day.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: That's right.
audioscript.speaker: SOPHIE

audioscript.text: No, I just got a normal return ticket.
audioscript.speaker: SOPHIE
audioscript.explain: Q4: The man assumes it wasn't a *'season ticket'*. Sophie agrees and says *'I just got a normal return ticket'*. The question already has *'standard'*, so the missing word is **return**.

audioscript.text: I don't have a rail card, so I didn't get any discount.

audioscript.text: I keep meaning to get one, because it's a lot cheaper.

audioscript.text: Part 3.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will hear two students of social history called Annie and Jack discussing their presentation about refrigeration.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: OK, Jack.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: Before we plan our presentation about refrigeration, let's discuss what we've discovered so far.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: Fine, Annie.
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: Though I have to admit I haven't done much research yet.
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: Nor me.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: But I found an interesting article about ice houses.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: I'd seen some 18th- and 19th-century ones here in the UK, so I knew they were often built in a shady area.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: Or underground, close to lakes that might freeze in the winter.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: Then blocks of ice could be cut and stored in the icehouse.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: But I didn't realize that insulating the blocks with straw or sawdust meant they didn't melt for months.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE
audioscript.explain: Q21: Annie says she *'didn't realize that insulating the blocks with straw or sawdust meant they didn't melt for months'* — **'insulating'** means keeping the cold in, so this explains **how the ice was kept frozen**. The question asks what she discovered, and this was her surprise. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: The ancient Romans had refrigeration too.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: I didn't know that.
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: Yes, pits were dug in the ground, and snow was imported from the mountains.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: Even though they were at quite a distance, the snow was stored in the pits.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: Ice formed at the bottom of it, both the ice and the snow were then sold.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE
audioscript.explain: Q22: The passage says *'both the ice and the snow were then sold'* — this means refrigeration became a **commercial business** where people bought and sold ice and snow. ***Option B is a trap*** — the snow came *'from the mountains'* which were *'at quite a distance'*, not nearby. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: The ice cost more than the snow, and my guess is that only the wealthy members of society could afford it.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: I wouldn't be surprised.
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: I also came across an article about modern domestic fridges.
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: Several different technologies are used, but they were too complex for me to understand.
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: You have to wonder what happens when people get rid of old ones.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: You mean because the gases in them are harmful for the environment?
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: Exactly.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: At least there are now plenty of organizations that will recycle most of the components safely, but of course some people just dump old fridges in the countryside.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE
audioscript.explain: Q23: Jack says *'some people just dump old fridges in the countryside'* — **'dump'** means throw away carelessly, which is **irresponsible disposal**. Annie agrees this is a problem. ***Option C is wrong*** — they say fridges *'hardly ever break down'*, so they do NOT worry about them breaking quickly. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: It's hard to see how they can be stopped unfortunately.
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: In the UK, we get rid of 3 million a year altogether.
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: That sounds a lot, especially because fridges hardly ever break down.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: That's right.
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: In this country, we keep domestic fridges for 11 years on average.
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: And a lot last for 20 or more.
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: So if you divide the cost by the number of years you can use a fridge, they're not expensive compared with some household appliances.
audioscript.speaker: JACK
audioscript.explain: Q24: Jack explains *'if you divide the cost by the number of years you can use a fridge, they're not expensive'* — this means over time, fridges are **good value for money**. Annie agrees with *'True'*. ***Option B is not their main point*** — they mention colors and designs but do not agree these are useful variations. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: True.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: I suppose manufacturers encourage people to spend more by making them different colors and designs.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: I'm sure when my parents bought their first fridge, they had hardly any choice.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: Yes, there's been quite a change.
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Right, let's make a list of topics to cover in our presentation, and decide who's going to do more research on them.
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: Then later we can get together and plan the next step.
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: OK, how about starting with how useful refrigeration is, and the range of goods that are refrigerated nowadays?
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: Because of course, it's not just food and drinks.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: No, I suppose flowers and medicines are refrigerated, too.
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: And computers. I could do that.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE
audioscript.explain: Q25: Annie says *'And computers. I could do that'* — **'I could do that'** means she volunteers to research this topic. The topic is **the goods that are refrigerated**, which includes computers. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: Unless you particularly want to.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: No, that's fine by me.
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: What about the effects of refrigeration on people's health?
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: After all, some of the chemicals used in the 19th century were pretty harmful.
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: But there have been lots of benefits too, like always having access to fresh food.
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: Do you fancy dealing with that?
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: I'm not terribly keen to be honest.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: Hmm, nor me.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: My mind just goes blank when I read anything about chemicals.
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: Oh, all right then, I'll do you a favor, but you owe me, Jack.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE
audioscript.explain: Q26: Annie says *'Oh, all right then, I'll do you a favor'* — she agrees to research **the effects on health** even though she is not keen. **'I'll do'** means she takes the task. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: OK?
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: What about the effects on food producers, like farmers in poorer countries being able to export their produce to developed countries?
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: Something for you maybe?
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: I don't mind, it should be quite interesting.
audioscript.speaker: JACK
audioscript.explain: Q27: Jack says *'I don't mind, it should be quite interesting'* — **'I don't mind'** means he agrees to research **the impact on food producers**. Annie offered it to him, and he accepts. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: I think we should also look at how refrigeration has helped whole cities, like Las Vegas, which couldn't exist without refrigeration, because it's in the middle of a desert.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: Right.
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: I had a quick look at an economics book in the library that's got a chapter about this sort of thing.
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: I could give you the title if you want to do this section.
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: Not particularly to be honest.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: I find economics books pretty heavy going as a rule.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: OK, leave it to me then.
audioscript.speaker: JACK
audioscript.explain: Q28: Jack says *'OK, leave it to me then'* — **'leave it to me'** means he will research **the impact on cities**. Annie did not want to do it, so Jack takes over. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: Thanks.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: Then there's transport, and the difference that refrigerated trucks have made.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: I wouldn't mind having a go at that.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE
audioscript.explain: Q29: Annie says *'I wouldn't mind having a go at that'* — **'having a go'** means she wants to try researching **refrigerated transport**. Jack does not object. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: Don't forget trains too.
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: I read something about milk and butter being transported in refrigerated railroad cars in the USA, right back in the 1840s.
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: I hadn't thought of trains. Thanks.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: Should we have a separate section on domestic fridges?
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: After all, they're something everyone's familiar with.
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: What about splitting it into two?
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE

audioscript.text: You could investigate 19th and 20th century fridges, and I'll concentrate on what's available these days, and how manufacturers differentiate their products from those of their competitors.
audioscript.speaker: ANNIE
audioscript.explain: Q30: Jack says *'You could investigate 19th and 20th century fridges, and I'll concentrate on what's available these days'* — **'you'** means Annie, and **'I'** means Jack, so they split the topic of **domestic fridges** between them. This means **both Annie and Jack** do research. So the answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: OK, that suits me.
audioscript.speaker: JACK

audioscript.text: That is the end of part 3.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER
